q: A camera is an optical instrument that forms and records an image of an object.
e: True. A camera forms and records an image of an object on film or on an electronic sensor. A convex lens throws a real inverted image onto that screen. Magnetic or thermal sensors are not the usual picture-taker.

q: The image may be recorded on film or it may be detected by an electronic sensor that stores the image analogously.
e: False. An electronic sensor stores the image digitally, as pixels, not analogously. Film is the chemical analogue record. Digital cameras replaced that film with a pixel array.

q: A convex lens focuses the light from the object to form a real inverted image on the film or electronic sensor.
e: True. A concave lens diverges and will not form that real film image. Focusing then slides the lens distance until the image is sharp. The camera's convex lens converges light to a real inverted image on the film or sensor.

q: A diaphragm is placed in front of the convex lens to control the amount of light energy falling on the film.
e: False. The diaphragm is placed behind the convex lens to control how much light hits the film. In front would be the wrong side of the focusing element. Amount of light is its job; time is the shutter's job.

q: The aperture is a circular opening through which the light passes.
e: True. Bright light wants a large f-number; dim light wants a small one. Aperture is the circular opening light passes through. f-number is focal length over diameter; smaller f-number means a wider hole.

q: The size or the diameter of the aperture is expressed in terms of f-numbers.
e: True. Small f-number, wide aperture, more light. Bright scenes need a large f-number so the hole is stopped down. f-number is focal length of the lens divided by aperture diameter.

q: The f-number of a camera is the ratio of the diameter of aperture to the focal length of the lens.
e: False. f-number is focal length divided by aperture diameter, f/D, not D/f. A small f-number is a wide hole. Bright light wants a large f-number so the hole is stopped down.

q: The smaller the f-number, the wider the aperture is.
e: True. f-number is focal length of the lens divided by aperture diameter. Small f-number, wide aperture, more light. Bright scenes need a large f-number so the hole is stopped down.

q: When taking a photograph in bright light a small f-number (wide aperture) must be used.
e: False. Bright light needs a large f-number, meaning a narrow aperture, so the film is not flooded. Small f-number, wide aperture, is for dim light. The diaphragm is how you make that change.

q: When taking a photograph in dim light a small f-number (wide aperture) must be used.
e: True. Bright scenes need a large f-number so the hole is stopped down. f-number is focal length of the lens divided by aperture diameter. Small f-number, wide aperture, more light.

q: A shutter controls the time during which light enters the camera through the lens.
e: True. The shutter controls how long light may enter through the lens. Shutter speed is quoted as that exposure time. Shorter exposure is a higher shutter speed; focal length is a different knob.

q: The shutter speed is expressed in terms of the focal length.
e: False. Shutter speed is quoted as exposure time, not as focal length. Focal length belongs to the lens and to the f-number. Short exposure is a high shutter speed.

q: The shorter the exposure time, the higher the shutter speed is.
e: True. The shutter times how long light may enter through the lens. Shutter speed is quoted as that exposure time. A short exposure is a high shutter speed; focal length is a different control.

q: A camera consists of a focusing ring by which the distance between the lens and the film can be adjusted to obtain a sharp image on the film.
e: True. It is not a brightness control. Wrong distance leaves the picture blurred. The focusing ring changes lens-to-film distance until the image is sharp.

q: The film consists of a thin layer of chemical compounds of gold.
e: False. Photographic film uses silver compounds, not gold. Those silver grains blacken where light hits. Digital sensors then replace the whole chemical layer with pixels.

q: In a digital camera, the film is replaced by an electronic sensor made up of millions of tiny pixels which response to light.
e: True. Diodes or grains are not the name of those picture elements. A digital sensor is millions of tiny pixels that respond to light. They store the image digitally, not analogously.
